### Units of my system

My hamiltoninan $H(u)=H(x_1,x_2,p_1,p_2)$ is given by the electromagnetic interaction potential $V(x_1,x_2)$, and the reflecting boundaries potnetial $V_b$, and of course the kinetic terms $T(p_i)$

$$H(u)=\frac{p_1^2}{2m_1}+\frac{p_2^2}{2m_2}+\frac{\mathcal{C}}{|x_1-x_2|}+V_b(x_1)+V_b(x_2)$$

Where as $V_b(x_i)$ is to be understood as a refelecting boundary $\partial \mathcal{B}$ that traps particle $i$, so $x_i\in\mathcal{B}$. So when $x_i$ crosses the boundary the conjugate momentum is inverted $p_i \to -p_i$.
Motivated by thermodynamical settings, in which two isolated systems exchange heat, we considere a partition on $\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}(1) \cup \mathcal{B}(2)$, with no overlap $\mathcal{B}(1)\cap \mathcal{B}(2)=\emptyset$. We define the boundary in coordinates by an open interval $\mathcal{B}(i)=(b_i-L,b_i+L)$, with boundaries at $\partial\mathcal{B}=b_i\pm L$. The partition is created by choosing $b_1 < b_2$ sattisfying $b_1+L < b_2-L$. A result of the partitioning is a serperation distance $\delta = b_1+L- (b_2-L)=b_1-b_2+2>0$. 

The boundary potential can then be defined as
$$V_b(x_i) =\Bigg\{\begin{matrix} 0 & \text{ if } x_i \in \mathcal{B}(i),\\
\infty & \text{ if } x_i \not\in \mathcal{B}(i).
\end{matrix}
$$

The hamiltonian for inside the boundary $x_1,x_2 \in \mathcal{B}$, then becomes
$$H(u)=\frac{p_1^2}{2m_1}+\frac{p_2^2}{2m_2}+\frac{C}{|x_1-x_2|}$$

I want to investigate the characteristic units of my system. As my boundary defines a characteristic length scale $L$, to which the particle positions are confind to. I will write the units of the dimesion in brackets, i.e. meters $[\text{m}]$

$$
\begin{align}
x [\text{m}] \to \hat{x}[\text{L}]&=\tfrac{x}{L} [\text{L}] \\
\Leftrightarrow x [\text{m}] &= L\hat{x}  
\end{align}
$$

How did this effect my Hamiltonina $H$? The interaction term gets transformed:
$$V(x_1-x_2)= \frac{\mathcal{C}}{|x_1-x_2|}= \frac{\mathcal{C}/L}{|\hat{x}_1-\hat{x}_2|}$$

This results in a natural units of energy to be given by the relation of the characteristic interaction strength $\mathcal{C}$ per characteristic length scale $L$. So we considere in relation to the $\mathcal{C}/L$: 
$$\frac{H(u)}{\mathcal{C}/L} =  \frac{p_1^2}{2m_1\,\mathcal{C}/L}+\frac{p_2^2}{2m_2\,\mathcal{C}/L}+\frac{1}{|\hat{x}_1-\hat{x}_2|}=\frac{E}{\mathcal{C}/L}.$$

With the dimensions of energy given by $\mathcal{C}/L$.

How about the units of momentum and time?
Energy is in units $E_{\text{sys}}[\mathcal{C}/L]$ and in units of length $L$, mass $\text{}$ and time $\text{t}$, $E_{\text{SI}}[(L/\text{t})^2\text{m}]$ we can equate these $E_{\text{sys}}=E_{\text{SI}}$ to obtain the units of time:

$$\begin{align}
1[(L/\text{t})^2\text{m}]&=1[\mathcal{C}/L]\\
1[\text{t}^2] &=1[L^3\text{m}/\mathcal{C}]
\end{align}$$

Here a suggestion, without much thought: As a simple model, I will set $m_1=m_2=1\text{m}$ so that both point mass are the same, and would simplify my units for the system.

### surface of section

Yet again, considering the boundary of the surface of section:
The surface of section will be a plane which position depends on the sign of the characteristic interaction strenght $\mathcal{C}$. 
If $\mathcal{C}<0$ then the ineraction is repulsive and the boundaries further apart, are sure to make contact, where as the opposite is the case for $\mathcal{C}>0$. Thus, without loss of generality, we choose particle $1$ as the conditional particle. Depending on the sign of the characteristic interaction strenght $\mathcal{C}$ either $\partial \mathcal{B}(1,1)$ ($\mathcal{C}<0$, repulsive) or $\partial \mathcal{B}(1,2)$ ($\mathcal{C}>0$, attractive) will mark the point that span the surface of section $\Sigma=\text{span}(x_2,p_2)$. We shall refere to the boundary of particle $1$ as $\partial \mathcal{B}(1,\_)=\partial \mathcal{B}=\{-(1+\delta),-\delta\}$

**Finding the boundary**
Remember that the kinetic energy term is positive $T(p_i)\geq 0$ for all $p_i$. 
$$\begin{align}
H(u)=T(p_1)+T(p_2)+V(x_1,x_2)&=E\\
\Rightarrow T(p_2)+ V(\partial \mathcal{B}(j),x_2)&\leq E
\end{align}$$

We are seeking all points $\{(x_2,p_2)|T(p_2)+ V(\partial \mathcal{B}(j),x_2)-E=0\}$.

The code, scans through the range of $x_2\in\mathcal{B}(2)$ and determine all $p_2$ that sattisfy this condition.

``` Julia
function boundary(E; p=(; C=-1.0, m1=1.0, m2=1.0, L=1.0, del=DEL_BOX), n=400)
    dB  = get_boxes(p)
    x1  = p.C > 0 ? dB[1][1] : dB[1][2]          # section: particle 1 fixed here
    x2  = range(dB[2][1], dB[2][2]; length=n)    # sweep all of box 2

    p2 = map(x2) do x
        K = E - V_int([x1, x, NaN, NaN], p)      # kinetic energy available (p1 = 0)
        K >= 0 ? sqrt(2p.m2 * K) : NaN           # NaN = forbidden, breaks the line
    end

    upper = Point2f.(x2, p2)
    lower = Point2f.(reverse(x2), -reverse(p2))
    return vcat(upper, lower, upper[1:1])        # closed curve
end
```


### Observations of the two charged particles serperated by boxes



![$\mathcal{C}=-1$: Boundary of the section for the two-box system. We observe the minimal energy accessible to the system!](../../figures/two-boxed-charges/section-boundary/C-1-boundaries_of_section.png)

![$\mathcal{C}=+1$:Boundary of the section for the two-box system. We observe the minimal energy accessible to the system!](../../figures/two-boxed-charges/section-boundary/C1-boundaries_of_section.png)


The figure shows the boundary of the Poincaré section for the repulsive two-particle system, with particle 1 fixed at the selected boundary point and particle 2 sampled across its allowed box. The closed curve is obtained by solving the energy constraint
$$
T(p_2) + V(\partial \mathcal{B}, x_2) = E
$$
for each position $x_2$ in the second box. The accessible states lie inside the enclosed region, while the curve itself marks the phase-space boundary where the kinetic energy available to particle 2 vanishes. This construction makes explicit how the fixed boundary condition on particle 1 defines a reduced two-dimensional section of the full four-dimensional dynamics.

When varying the parameter $\mathcal{C}$ from negative we observe no converging behaviour, as to be expected.
